utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If I could remind you, Mr. Limaj, of the affirmation you gave at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, before I continue, there were just two brief matters to take up with the Court. The first is with respect to the observation of counsel that was made at the end of the evening yesterday, the basis for a question that I put to the witness. I have discussed it with Defence counsel. We have, I think it's fair to say, agreed to disagree but in that way we have settled it and need not take up any more time of the Chamber with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sounds almost as good as some of the decisions we've had to give.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The second issue has to do with scheduling. And I don't know if this has already been raised with the Court, but there is a plan to interpose a witness and I maybe allow Defence counsel to raise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution are very kindly agreed because of the general difficulties of timing to interpose this afternoon - I think not this session, the next session - the expert who we have brought here from commitments abroad. I'm afraid it's the only week he could be here. To allow for time for cross-examination as well as any other questions. It would be desirable to make a start on him today because he has to be away by tomorrow night. He in fact arrived at the beginning of the week. His name is Mr. Churcher and you do have his report. I am obliged to the Prosecution for allowing us to do that. I'm sorry it's split up a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, well, circumstances obviously warrant that course being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, do you recall being present in Kroimire on the 17th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there in one of the battles when he came out publicly. I think that must be the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't have the right channel on here. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were there in Kroimire because there was fighting there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Kroimire because fighting had taken place there, and I went to visit to see how they were, how everything was, because that was the first battle. In the evening I went to visit them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Haxhi Shala was with you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Haxhi Shala and someone else. I think we were two or three persons. We went there by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you returned from Kroimire to Klecke, you took with you Ramadan Behluli. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't recollect it very well. I accept what Ramadan has said. Personally, I don't have anything special to add to that, because myself I can't remember everything accurately.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that on this occasion Haxhi Shala and someone else. The someone else in -- was identified or described, I should say, by Ramadan Behluli as the driver. Do you recall who the driver was?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Haxhija was the driver, Haxhija was on the wheel. He is known as a professional driver; this I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he -- was -- did he drive you places on other occasions?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There have been other occasions. We were friends. Some of us took the wheel, but not necessarily him. Sometimes it has been him. Sometimes I have driven myself. Sometimes someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate you say that your memory of this event is not particularly clear, but do you recall on this occasion or any other occasion telling Ramadan Behluli that if he saw the Serb police approaching his position in Carraleve he should not wait for orders but he should attack? Do you recall telling him that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Prosecutor, no. No, Ramadan has not said what you are putting to me. I didn't need to give any orders because every member of the KLA was there to attack the Serbian forces. I didn't need to give any orders. They were there for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj -- Mr. Limaj. Why don't you just tell me what you remember, if you remember at all, what you said to Ramadan Behluli on this subject.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what we had discussed in real terms, but what you are putting to me about attacking the Serb forces when they -- if they come to Carraleve, that doesn't -- that is not true. As I said, no member of the KLA had need for any orders to attack the Serbian forces because it was known to all that they were there for that. I can't tell you specifically what I've told him. I don't remember. Because this was nothing of any importance for me to remember. All the time we took -- we discussed with soldiers, not only with Ramadan, we always discussed such issues, how things were, what they had been doing, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I want to ask you some questions about the 121 Brigade. You testified on the third day of your testimony, it's at page 39, that - and tell me if I'm summarising your testimony correctly - that soldiers who were part of units that later became the 121 Brigade and who were killed before the 121 Brigade was formed at the beginning of August were later considered to be part of the 121 Brigade. Is that a fair summary of what your testimony was on the third day on this point? I can say it again if you ...

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time, yes. But we maybe specified better. Most of it is as you put it to me. But if you allow me, I could specify it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, all the soldiers who had laid down their lives as martyrs at various periods of time before the structuring of the KLA, before its organisation, on the place they were killed, depending on the unit they operated, and the brigade that covered that territory, all those martyrs were later considered as martyrs of the units which formed a brigade. And they are considered martyrs of the brigade in the territory they were killed and which covered that territory, depending on the unit they fought and depending which brigade comprised that unit because we have soldiers that were killed at different points of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. So -- now, this is something that occurred for martyrs, people who were killed during the war. Correct? You've talked about this being for martyrs.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For the concrete case we are talking, it is for martyrs, for the martyrs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj, have you ever said you were a commander of the 121 Brigade in June or July of 1998, at that time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What time do you mean? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you ever described yourself as being a commander of the -- you made the point about martyrs and now I'm asking about yourself. Have you ever said that you were a commander of the 121 Brigade in June or July of 1998? Do you recall ever saying that? Is that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we look at it from a later perspective, all the developments that occurred in that region, they were described as linked with the Brigade 121. In this context it is possible that I may have said that the members of Brigade 121st, without referring to a specific date. So in this context, it is possible that I have said what you put to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you're telling us that you have not then said with respect to a specific date that you were a commander of the 121 Brigade before August of 1998. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I am trying to sum up developments. Let's talk about the logistical base, not only about the martyrs. And when we talk about the logistics, for example, of Brigade 121st, that is based on this place, on that place. So without specifying the time, it is possible to say this. I am trying to explain to you that nothing concrete happened before Brigade 121st, because before the brigade was formed there were units of villages. And within villages, there were several units. So you couldn't refer to them -- to each and every one of them in particular. So you talk in general about Brigade 121st because that is as a landmark for us when we talk about that period, about those developments. So in this context, it is possible that I have said what you told me, Mr. Prosecutor. I can't tell you for sure. I'm looking at it from this perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, isn't it the case that you could talk about the 121 Brigade with relation to events in June and July 1998 because, in fact, when the 121 Brigade was given its name in August of 1998, nothing changed; it was simply -- the structure remained the same. It was just given a name in August of 1998. So for that reason, you could talk about -- you and others can talk about events in June and July of 1998 as being -- involving the 121 Brigade, because for all respects except for name, the 121 Brigade existed at that time. Isn't that in fact the case?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well, Mr. Prosecutor, I know very well what Shukri Buja said in his interview. You are very clear about that. You know that Shukri Buja said he was zone commander on the 3rd of July. He showed you the villages, the region he was responsible for. How is it possible for a zone commander -- he was appointed to form that zone. How is it possible that a commander of Nerodime zone has also Brigade 121st? You must know it very well because you have had the facts in front of you. There was no Brigade 121st. What you are staying, it was intended to be the Nerodime zone, and I think Shukri Buja mentioned that in his testimony. He said, I was appointed as a zone commander and he indicated the zone and the municipalities. It cannot be that a brigade of one zone covers another zone; it cannot be. How can that be, please, that a unit commander gives orders to a zone commander? You don't need any military rationale to draw such conclusions. How can brigade commander, even that commander, give orders to a zone commander? You know very well that you have the Pastrik zone commander, Nerodime zone commander, and you are trying to present me as a region commander. Then why didn't I become the commander of the Pastrik zone? If I was such a commander, then why should someone else give orders to me? Please, facts speak differently. You know the facts very well and I'm surprised that you want to misinterpret them --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, the answer to my question is: No, you don't agree that the reason people talk about the 121st Brigade in relation to June and July 1998 is because the structure was, in effect, in place already by that time? The answer to that question is no from you. Right? You don't agree with what I have stated?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no brigade structure. There was no brigade. Even -- it didn't exist as a perception, as an idea at that time. Even the elements of such brigade, as you are saying, existed. That is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, in June of 1998 you presided over an oath ceremony in Klecke?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And also --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end of June I think it was or beginning of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And also present were Muse Jashari and Kumanova. Right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Muse Jashari, Ismet Jashari, and outside there were others. There were representatives of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Who were the representatives of the General Staff who were present?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not filmed because that was shown, broadcast, on television. But the cameras didn't film the other persons. It was Hashim Thaqi, chairman of the Democratic Party; it was also Sokol Bashota; Kadri Veseli; and two officers whom I have mentioned earlier, Agim Xhelaj and Byslym Zyropi. But the camera didn't focus on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said it was broadcast on television. I take it it was broadcast on Albanian television, television from Albania?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, because that was the first programme. It was for the first time it was shown on television. A special programme was programmed on -- for television broadcast for the KLA. Kosova saw it for the first time. The General Staff -- I don't know how they managed to have a television crew come there. They wanted to prepare such a programme, so we improvised there, the environment. Like, we organised an oath ceremony. They visited some positions, but that is the first programme prepared deliberately for -- to make public the KLA. That was an exclusive feature, if I might say so. It was an agreement between the General Staff and the television crew.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it broadcast shortly after it was filmed at that time? It was broadcast at the same time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I think it was broadcast after four or five days or a week, because we couldn't broadcast it in Kosova; we had to send it to Albania. And it was broadcast by the Albanian television. I don't know how they transported it to Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was broadcast from Albania, but it could be watched on television in Kosovo. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, through satellite antennas or satellite dishes. That was the only way of communication. Whoever had a satellite dish could receive such programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The oath ceremony that took place, was that a real oath ceremony or was it one that was staged for television?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you remember, when we discussed this, I remember I talked about this either with you or the Defence lawyers, when we talked about the rules. The rules contains the oath ceremony. After we took hold of these rules, before that, the 20th of June, we don't have any oath ceremony. So an organised form of oath, we didn't have before that time. After we received the rules, we started to organise these oath ceremonies. With relation to this specific case, I am telling you that we staged it for television programme -- in fact, there were people who really took the oath, but it was organised then because there were people from various units present because we wanted the story to look as nice as possible on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So there were people -- the people who were took place -- took part in the oath ceremony were not just from Klecke; there were soldiers from other units in the area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the General Staff had talked with about the coverage in Drenica and elsewhere, so they had collected some soldiers and weapons. I saw some weapons that day for the first time; they were there just for the purposes of being shown on television. I never saw them after that day. For us, it was a problem to have uniforms because we didn't want the soldiers to appear on television without uniforms. Some soldiers, as I said, came from various places. There were my soldiers, soldiers from Kumanova, some soldiers from Drenice who came along with some of the representatives of the General Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were any soldiers from Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been -- there may have been some soldiers. I don't remember. You must bear in mind that most of the soldiers were my own soldiers, so I don't -- I didn't care about the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You've answered the question. In June of 1998, there was also a large funeral with a march that took place in Carralluke.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you a little clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is from the beginning of P -- Exhibit P35, and if we could switch to the Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, is that the funeral march in Carralluke?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we of course see you in the march. Is that Isak Musliu who is behind you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you rewind it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. We'll play it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. The second person on the right. It -- as you look at it. Behind me is Shaban Shala.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just going to continue playing it and if you recognise anyone else, could you tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is difficult to distinguish them -- Gani Koci. I see him. It's not very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. If you -- we'll just continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are soldiers. One I could tell, he was from Suhareke municipality; his name is Isuf Krasniqi, I think. There are many from Malisheve, many. Most of them are from Malisheve. But there are also people from Drenice, from all parts of Kosova I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The funeral was for a man by the name of Ymer Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he was killed on the 16th of June, 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date very well. I thought it was on the 9th. Maybe it is on the 16th. I can't tell for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This march, though, took place in June. Correct? It took place some -- a few days after -- whether it was the 9th or the 16th, it took place a few days after the funeral?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After -- if he was killed on the 16th, probably two or three days after.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this march was also broadcast on television. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want -- if you allow me, I want to explain. That day I didn't know, but I found out later. When we went to the burial place, we saw thousands of reporters. Someone prevented them from going to the place where the corpse was, the coffin was. Someone from the General Staff, I don't know who it was, allowed only the reporter of the Albanian television to film this grave. Only this part is recorded. One minute or two minutes were reported, because no journalist -- no foreign journalists were allowed to record anything at the burial place. Maybe five or six seconds someone has managed to film, but as far as I know it was the same journalist who was allowed to film there one or two minutes, only that part that is shown here. And we were told that a brief recording would take place, and we prepared that line of soldiers that you see there to be filmed also for propaganda purposes, for the world to see that there was an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand your testimony correctly. The -- what you're saying is that the person -- the Albanian -- you think that the Albanian television journalist filmed that portion of the march and also some portion -- brief portion of the burial site, and that that was -- those -- those portions were broadcast on Albanian television. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Maybe I wasn't clear. I will try to be clearer this time because this -- at this time KLA members were reserved. As for -- as far as media is concerned, they didn't want to contact the media and they didn't know how to behave with the media. It was like this: There were hundreds of journalists. Here you cannot see the burial site, and at the burial site there were hundreds of journalists, both foreign and from the country but they were not allowed to film. Only the cameraman from the Albanian television was allowed to film. But as for whether he then sold this story to EuroNews or other news agencies, I don't know. I don't know what happened afterwards. What I know is this person was allowed to be next to the KLA columns and he can film them from there; and as for other journalists, foreign journalists, they were not allowed to film at the burial site. I don't know why they were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But the footage that we've just seen, that was broadcast on Albanian television, wasn't it? Do you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was broadcast. There is no spot in some clips that this scene is not used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to talk you about Sadik Shala, or ask you some questions, I should say, about Sadik Shala. He -- he is one of these -- one of the people you were describing earlier who was killed -- he was killed on the 19th of July, 1998, but he's sometimes described as being a member of the 121st Brigade. Correct? Does he -- is he one of those people you were talking about earlier, a martyr who ...

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I describe Sadik Shala? I cannot say that Sadik Shala was a unit leader because --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that later became 121 Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and it was one of the cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question simply was: Was he -- after he -- after the war, has he sometimes been described as being a member of the 121 Brigade? Right? He has been sometimes.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell me what his duties were -- was he -- was he in your unit in Klecke before he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I said earlier, we settled at Sadik's house and he covered all the expenses for us for two or three months while we were acting in profound illegality. After two or three months, things changed and Sadik started to procure supplies for the unit there, and not only for us, for others as well because he supported his extended family and it was easy for him to support my soldiers and other soldiers as well. And he gave all his fortune for the KLA. I can here tell you an example --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- he presented the KLA with cattle at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, just focus on the questions. So he provided supplies to the soldiers in your unit and in other units as well?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said that he helped everyone. Whoever he could help, he helped them. He helped soldiers. He helped others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So does that mean he helped soldiers in your unit and soldiers in other units as well? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my unit, I was staying in his unit and whoever asked him for help, he helped them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did he provide help for other units?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he helped soldiers and other units, whoever asked for help, and I am repeating this for the third or fourth time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to play a little clip from Exhibit P34, which is the documentary of his life. I'm going to play a little portion of it. It's clip 2. It starts at page 4 of the exhibit. Before we play it, Mr. Limaj, I'm going to ask that you pay attention to what Lahi Brahimaj says about the tasks of Sadik Shala because I'm going to ask you some questions about that. So if you could listen carefully to what he says, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, in the last sentence of what Lahi Brahimaj says about what Sadik Shala did it says: "At the same time Sadik Shala provisioned Celiku's units," units, "in the Pastrik Operation Zone, but he also performed some services for the KLA General Staff."

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said, Mr. Prosecutor, approximately because this is a documentary and everybody's trying to present him at his best, although he doesn't know all things as they were. Sadik Shala helped soldiers in different units because he had the means to do that. The tendency to present him as one who was a sector leader of the KLA units, this is not true. The truth is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, what I'm focussed on is that he said "Celiku's units." You had more than one unit; you were responsible for more than one unit, not just the unit in Klecke. But he supplied Celiku's units. That's in fact what he did, didn't he? He supplied your units?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. You're trying to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- say something else here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No. I'm saying what's on the tape. Do you have any explanation for how -- why Lahi Brahimaj said "Celiku's units," if that's not what in fact was the truth?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I have. First of all, Lahi Brahimaj at that time was never there. Do you know where he was active, where he operated? And he has no idea what was going on in that area. He was in a totally different area, in a Dukagjini zone, which is 80 kilometres far from our area. So he wasn't at all at that time in our area. He rarely came there. Your tendency, secondly, to present units as joint units, this is not correct. He did help. He helped everyone. He helped people in Malisheve, in Suhareke, in Drenice. He helped hundreds of thousands of people. Your Honours, he sent tonnes of flour to Drenica and you cannot now label him as someone who had been tasked to do such a thing because his personality was such. He for all his life helped people. He was rich, he and his family, and he had the means to people. He helped soldiers; he helped units. But the tendencies to present him as a supplier of all units, as someone who was tasked to do that, this is not true. As for Lahi, I already told you that he was not there at that time. And I don't know why he said that. You personally know that Lahi Brahimaj at that time was in Dukagjin. You know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I want to talk about Lapusnik. You testified that the -- that the KLA was - and I'm quoting your words. It's from the third day on page 69 - that the "KLA was concentrated in Lapusnik." That was your testimony. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, after the Lapusnik gorge was taken that the KLA units were positioned on the gorge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And -- and the unit that was in Lapusnik below the Peja-Pristina road was the Celiku 3 unit. Correct? It was known as the Celiku 3 unit? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: By one of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- you testified that the five positions that you identified on the map were within -- that those were all -- those were five positions of the Celiku 3 unit. Right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be so because that line of front was covered by soldiers from Celiku 3, and later on another unit covered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was that? Later on another unit covered that? You mean after the end of July 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I meant was along that front line, the front line that is connected with Celiku 3; that is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's try to be clear here. The five positions that you identified on the map, and we can put the map in front of you again if you like, but those five positions were Celiku 3 positions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And those were Celiku 3 positions in June and July of 1998, until the fall of the Lapusnik gorge. Right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Starting in May of 1998, Isak Musliu was the commander of Celiku 3. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We should explain this to the very end, how this happened. If you want to know the truth, if you're interested in the truth. But if you just want to go to the bottom line, Isak Musliu was commander of Celiku 3 unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. When you went to Lapusnik with Byslym Zyropi and Agim Qelaj to observe the unit you met with Isak Musliu and Ymer Alushani. Correct? That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Byslym Zyropi, Agim Qelaj, and someone else, I don't know who, they went to visit all the points and as part of their visit they visited Celiku 3 for 10, 15 minutes. I was with them. I was with them also on the other side of the terrain in Drenica. I also was with them in Aqareve [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please focus on my questions. I know you understand my questions. I know you're understanding them. Please focus on them and try to answer my questions. When you went to Celiku with Byslym Zyropi and Agim Qelaj you met with Ymer Alushani and Isak Musliu. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know that when soldiers -- when men came to Lapusnik to the Celiku 3 position to join the KLA, they were interviewed by Isak Musliu. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. What interview are we talking about here? He could not stop anyone from joining the KLA. My experience speaks differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me use a different word. They would meet with Isak Musliu. Correct? That would be the normal practice, to meet with Isak Musliu?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honours. I will tell you how it was. If someone had a friend, if someone had an uncle or a nephew or a relative, he immediately went to that friend or nephew or family member and joined the KLA immediately. At that time, volunteers were gathering to join the KLA. At that time it was just enough to have someone you know in the KLA and join. You could not stop anyone from joining. You could not prevent anyone from the right of joining the liberation war; the war was ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear, your testimony is: Men who came to Lapusnik, whether they knew somebody there or not, men who came to Lapusnik to join the KLA in June and July of 1998 were not normally met by Isak Musliu - that's your testimony - or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'm trying to explain to you a general experience. I'm not speaking here specifically for Lapusnik, but giving you a general picture, what happened here and there. I am sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, my question is about Lapusnik. Do you know the answer with respect to Lapusnik or not?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is what happened everywhere. Things did not happen differently in Lapusnik than in other places. Whoever wanted to join the KLA joined. This is my answer. This was how things worked at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember at this time period in June and July of 1998 that Chris Hill, Christopher Hill was the United States ambassador to Montenegro? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were aware that during the summer of 1998 that he was involved in trying to resolve matters between the -- in Kosovo, between the Serbs and the Albanians. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth at that time I didn't know it was Mr. Hill concretely. I knew it was an American who was dealing with this issue. Later on I knew that and I had the opportunity to meet him as well. Later on I learned he was the head of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: On your various trips to Lapusnik in June and July 1998 - and you've testified it was approximately 20; it might have been more, it might have been less - but on those various trips, did Isak Musliu tell you that he had met with Chris Hill at the barricade in Lapusnik at the end of June 1998? Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In this case to my knowledge it was Shaban Shala who met with him, not Isak. I don't know whether Isak accompanied Shaban Shala when he met with him; I don't know that. At that time Shaban Shala was there and Jakup was in a nearby village. This is to my knowledge -- you know who Shaban Shala is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yeah, I do. Jakup -- you're referring to Jakup Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said was that Jakup and Shaban Shala are co-villagers. They came from the same village. There is a road nearby Orlat-Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't remember Isak Musliu telling you that he had met and spoken to Christopher Hill and other US diplomats at the barricade? You don't remember that? He didn't tell you that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't tell me that and I don't think he knew him. We neither knew him because we didn't know the delegation at that time. For us it was a normal, ordinary diplomatic representatives who were visiting the area at that time. I don't think he knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well -- okay. Let me -- I'll ask you about that in a moment. But did you talk to -- let me just ask you this question: Did you talk to Shaban Shala about this meeting? You said you believed that Shaban Shala had the meeting. Did you talk to him about it? Mr. Limaj, it's a simple question. Yes or no, did you talk to Shaban Shala?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What makes you think he was the one who talked with Christopher Hill?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After developments later on, I think it was after the war, it was said that Shaban Shala discussed -- talked with him. If you remember Holbrooke's visit, this happened approximately at the same time and there is a notorious statement that was given at that time as well about Kijeva. Holbrooke proclaimed Kijeva as one of the most dangerous places at that time, and Kijeva is just 10 kilometres from Lapusnik. These were all words that were spoken around this time and this occasion. But later on, I don't know exactly when, it was said that it could have been Shaban Shala at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you meet with any of these US representatives during that time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. You're not telling me that a United States ambassador coming to Lapusnik in June of 1998 was an ordinary event, are you? That was -- that would in fact be an extraordinary event. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you that that in fact would be an extraordinary event, but thing is we didn't know. Holbrooke's visit was an extraordinary event, but he met with an ordinary soldiers. We didn't know who was coming in and who was going out. And you don't have information who is meeting who, as was the case with Mr. Holbrooke.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that you -- you knew nothing about Christopher Hill or any US representative coming to Lapusnik in June of 1998? You didn't know that. Is that your testimony? That did not come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it should be clear to you. At that time, I didn't know who was coming in, who was going out. Later on I learned, I learned from friends, from Jakup, or from someone else because such a visit was important for such a delegation to enter KLA territories. But for the event in question and for the day took place, I really don't know. I never really heard about it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: With respect to this visit of US representatives to Lapusnik at the -- on June 26th, 1998, do you remember when you learned about it and how you learned about it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this was not the visit to Lapusnik. I think you agree with me that this was not a visit to Lapusnik. This was a visit to Kijeva and Decan, I think. And they were passing through that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. The visit -- okay. The -- let me be more specific. It's a -- it's a -- a visit to the barricade on the Pristina-Peja road, the KLA barricade, at Lapusnik. Whether they went somewhere else afterwards, the point is -- the point is that they stopped at the barricade at Lapusnik and spent some time there. Do you -- did you -- did you learn of that and then --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Then my next question is: When did you learn of it and how did you learn of it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may have learned it in the meantime because I think it was a public demand made by Mr. Hill to open the road. It was a demand put forward by the delegation. So I don't remember when that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may err as to the timing, but I know what it is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I represent to you that the date was on the 26th of June, 1998, can you tell us approximately how long after the visit you learned of it? Was it within days? Was it within weeks? Months?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I learned about it when the meeting was with Jan Kickert with the European troika and the journalist Baton Haxhiu. It was then that I learned about the aim, but I can't tell you precisely when. But that was in the wake of these things that I mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That meaning --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- maybe even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That meeting that you just referred to with Jan Kickert was on the 30th of July. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were asking me about the 26th of July. I am not clear. I don't know when I learned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember how many days after the event happened that you learned about it? Was it within days? Weeks?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Really, I cannot tell you for certain. But to tell you the truth, that was not our concern. That was the business of those who were supposed to deal with that. So I can't tell you when I learned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, we've slipped from the 26th of June to the 26th of July. Perhaps we could get a clarification what it is you're putting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I'm putting is the 26th of June, and I think the witness misunderstood and thought it was the 26th of July. But it's the 26th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember if you learned about it before the fall of Lapusnik, before the 26th of July? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to think harder. I know about the famous statement by Mr. Holbrooke because that was an extraordinary event; it was all over the media. What I told you about Kijeva being the most dangerous place. I also know that they demanded the unblocking of Kijeve. But I don't know for sure when I heard about that because that was not my personal concern. I just know that I learned. I am trying to help you, but I cannot give you an exact time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, do you remember how you learned about it? Do you remember who told you about it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is -- I am trying to explain. I heard, probably from the media or from someone, from Mr. Krasniqi maybe, or we may have talked at the meeting with Jan Kickert later. I don't know exactly when. Really, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not our concern, to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, is it is it your best approximation that you went to -- between the 9th of May, 1998, and 26th of July, is it your best approximation - I know give or take one or a little bit - but it's your best approximation that you went to Lapusnik 20 times, as is stated in your pre-trial brief? Is that your best approximation?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you want it to be greater, the number, then let it be greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I just want the truth, Mr. Limaj. Your best approximation is 20, maybe more?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to tell you the truth, the truth that I know, but you haven't given me the opportunity before to tell me [as interpreted] the truth. If you had, I would have told you the truth earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm trying to give you every opportunity to give us your evidence, Mr. Limaj. Now, you testified that you went to -- one of the reasons you went to Lapusnik was that you went there on your way to Likovc.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I said one of the reasons. Sometimes I have gone there to visit Isak. I have visited other points. Sometimes I have gone to Likovc and on the way I have stopped and visited them. I said that was one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's how I put the question, but maybe it wasn't translated properly. Just to be clear, when you go from Klecke to Likovc you do not actually go through Lapusnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You go through Lapusnik, exactly. Exactly through Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but don't you in fact go from Klecke you go to Novoselle, you go to Terpeze --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Terpeze.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You go to the main road. You take a right --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orlat --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct? You get to the junction.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct? And if you're going to Likovc you continue driving across the Peja-Pristina road and you head towards Likovc. Can you explain to me how it is you would go to the right, go into Lapusnik, and that would somehow get you to Likovc?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. If you want me, I can draw or I can show it -- I can draw it. I can show you the route on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get the map.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that you are talking about only neighbourhoods -- one single neighbourhood of Lapusnik; you are not talking about the entire village. The village is very large.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put the question a little bit differently. You drew on a map - and I don't have the exhibit number at hand - but on one of the Defence exhibits you drew the road that you would take to come into Lapusnik. When you came into Lapusnik you drew the road -- it's from the Pristina-Peja road you drew the road that you would come down in -- to get into Lapusnik. Right? Do you remember drawing that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's better if I look at the map now and I can draw the road on it again to be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's DL4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: DL4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. And if it could be put on the ELMO, please. And it's not -- it shouldn't be that, but maybe -- the map I was thinking of is image 8 that he drew on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Image 8, that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh yeah, we have a copy of it here. If it could be put on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj, do you see -- you see the road that you drew red on that goes from the Pristina-Peja road into Lapusnik? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just point to it -- I believe it's DL8. I apologise on behalf of Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- Mr. Limaj, do you see the --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Just a second. I want to change this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't have a problem with the witness marking further this exhibit, but I don't -- it's a Defence exhibit. I don't know if -- no. Let me -- can I just first draw your attention -- there's a red line on the road that comes from the Peja-Pristina road to Lapusnik, into that part of Lapusnik. Do you see that? Do you see the -- okay --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you drew that red line as the road that you would take to come into -- that was the road that you took to come into Lapusnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I wanted to explain. You see this cross here? This is the cross. From here you can go to Isak's positions. That is the other road here, here. Here. It's like a crossroads which goes through Lapusnik village in this part here. Through the village of Lapusnik it goes to Damanek, Krajkove, Baince, Obrinje, Likovc. And the majority of Lapusnik, Your Honours, lies on this -- as a village lies on this part of the asphalt road. This is a very spread-out village. This is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, Mr. Limaj, if you're going to Likovc then you would come to the Orlat junction which is not on this map. Right? The Orlat junction is not on the map. Right? It's not on the map. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Then you would take a right on the Pristina-Peja road, you would come on to the map, then at that road you've just marked you would take a left to go to Likovc. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Next to that blue mark --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the witness doesn't have the exhibit in front of him; he has your copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, that's correct, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The markings to date have been in red. You are now wanting him to mark it further, I would suggest that it be in a different colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj thought of that and has a blue pen at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As always, you're both ahead of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, Mr. Limaj, can you just put -- can you just mark on this map where you marked -- had marked in blue before.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The line you're drawing in blue is the line -- the road you would take to go to Likovc. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- can -- just so the record is --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which goes through Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Just so the record is clear, can you just put an L next to the -- that blue line you've made.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And we'll understand that's an L for Likovc.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj -- so on your way to Likovc, then, you would not go down the road that you have drawn in red; that is going in another direction, to go down that road in red. Correct? That's not going to Likovc?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Who said that it goes Likovc? This goes to where I said yesterday, the day before yesterday, in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. So when you would stop in Lapusnik on your way to Likovc, you would go to the right instead of to the left at that intersection. Correct? And you would go into Lapusnik on that road that you have marked on red. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time one wanted to go to Likovc, you go this way. But sometimes you stopped on the way, met someone, had a coffee or a tea. At this junction, Your Honours, there were soldiers. You see these two lines, the red one and the blue one? There were soldiers at the junctions who could follow the movements of the cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you -- I think the point has been made, so I don't think you need the exhibit any -- or we'll leave it there for now. You -- you also said that when you went to Lapusnik from Klecka, the only way you would go is the way we just described, that is you would drive to Novoselle, Terpeze, to the -- to the highway. You take a right on - I call it the highway, the main road. You take a right to the Orlat junction and then you would come into Lapusnik this way. Is that the only way that you would go -- drive from Klecka to Lapusnik at this time, in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make it clearer, with the exception of the first time on the 9th of May when we came down the mountain to attack the Serb forces from Berisa village for the first time, with the exception of the 9th of May, usually the way to Lapusnik goes to where I have indicated. There is no motor road that goes from any other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Another way you could go to Lapusnik from Klecke would be to go to Sedlare/Shale, then drive up to Nekovc, and to Kishna Reka and then from you could take a back road to Lapusnik that came up right at the positions. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me that was an unknown path and very dangerous. It is true, as the Prosecutor is saying, from various villages, Kizhareke, Shale, Nekovce, you can go to Vukovic from Nekovce, you can go there. But that road was the target of the fire by the Serb and the KLA forces. For me, that was an entirely unknown terrain, whereas this road that I indicated was the normal, the usual one, because this was within our control, that was a safe passage for us. Sometimes soldiers used the path you indicated at night. But the main road was the one I showed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if you were travelling -- if you were driving from Carraleve to Lapusnik, what is the way you ordinarily would go then at that time? When you got to Shale -- would people normally go from Shale to Klecka and take the road you describe, or would they normally go from Shale to Nekovc and Kishna Reka? What's the road that people normally would take?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to explain here, Your Honours. There was not a road to Klecke -- a road as such because the infrastructure -- Klecke-Shale motor road. There wasn't any. That was a very bad road. It was late that we kind of built a road together with the villagers because that enabled us to move more freely. But in May/June it was impossible for cars to go there through this road. Villagers gradually started to build that road for us to manage to penetrate from Klecke to Shale. Even if you used the tractor you could use that road, but that, too, was very difficult. The road began to be built because Malisheve, which was under our control, the only supply line was from Pristina through -- using local roads to come to Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So until the road got fixed up, normally people would -- travellers would go from Carraleve to Shale, then Nekovc to Kisna Reka to Lapusnik. Correct? Until the road was fixed up and then --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It was impossible to go to Kishna Reka at that time. It was impossible because this was the front line there. There was constant fighting. What you're saying you had to go to Vukovc. What the Prosecutor is saying this is the road, this here. This is the road that he's saying, a road that links Kishna Reka, Shale, Nekovce, and then it comes to Kroimire and Carraleve. I don't know. And this is where the Serb forces were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, Mr. Limaj, before --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This road was under constant fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. But if you're coming from the south before you got to that portion of the road you could come behind to Lapusnik to where position 5 -- 4 and 5 were on a road from Kishna Reka -- you didn't need to take that road; you could take a road behind that would go up to position 4 and 5. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't believe it's on the map. I'm just asking you from your memory that there was a road -- you could go up from Kishna Reka directly up to position 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there is such a road. I don't know what has happened later. I don't know that such a road exists from Kishna Reka to come to Lapusnik. We saw the positions. You didn't have a road to link one village with another, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Your testimony is you don't know?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that there is such a road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There is an ordinance survey-type map which has got most of the roads on it. So if there is a road that is known to the Prosecutor, then perhaps he could point it out on DL4.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm interested in the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were asking by Mr. Mansfield to show on the map the places you went in Lapusnik. Do you recall being in Lapusnik for an oath ceremony during June of 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall that the oath ceremony took place in a yard across the road from a compound where the soldiers would ordinarily go to eat?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we look at this part, I think that day we couldn't see much of it. The place is very green. There are many pastures. We were on a pasture. There were some soldiers there; we took the oath. That is the truth. But if you look at Lapusnik, it is a place full of greenery. It has fields, pastures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe where in Lapusnik that oath ceremony took place?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot, Mr. Prosecutor. I cannot describe the exact place because every part is similar. There are all lawns and pastures all over. It was just a lawn, a meadow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you give a speech at the oath ceremony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I didn't give any speeches. Your Honours, I simply read the text of the oath, the way you see it on the -- on the clip. I was the one to read the military oath, then the soldiers repeated after me. Nothing else happened. After 15, 20 minutes they dispersed. After the ceremony was over, then I talked for a couple of minutes with the soldiers, how they were, how their families were, and that's it. I was the one who read the oath text.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Why did you read the oath text in -- at the oath ceremony in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to tell you why. Your Honours, you have a tradition and you should bear in mind the circumstances in my country. With your armies, you have a tradition, and maybe sometimes with your armies it's monotonous. But in our history it was the first time that we had the opportunity to read an oath ceremony text in Albanian language. It was not something formal, as it is with other armies. For us, it was a ceremony. It was a sign of respect. That's why we went to others when they organised their oath ceremonies. And to our tradition, you always give your guests the priority. Those young men there, they respected me, they thought it was important that I read the text. But, Mr. Prosecutor, I've read so many oath ceremony texts, I've read texts in Drenica, I went to other places. This was a celebration for us. This was the first opportunity for us to show that something serious was going on, that we were really going to form a real army. Civilians, family members took part in these ceremonies. There were people who fainted and needed medical treatment. They fainted because of joy. There was a person who was a former political prisoner who read the oath because we honoured that person, we gave him the opportunity to read it. You know, Mr. Prosecutor, hundreds of our soldiers were killed inside the Yugoslav army ranks. Our nation had never had the opportunity to read the ceremony -- oath ceremony in their native language.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I think you've answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume just after 4.00 and I gather that's the point at which you suggest, Mr. Mansfield, we might interpose the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Please. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being so, Mr. Limaj will understand and will take his place back in the body of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I could say I'll be taking the next witness. I have a short motion. I'm objecting to the introduction of one of the exhibits on the Defence's list for the next witness, so perhaps that should be done before the witness comes in so he doesn't have to sit through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We'll attend to that when we return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We were too hasty, Mr. Limaj. You can't have a break, it seems. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I think out of courtesy to Your Honours I should indicate that Mr. Whiting's very kind and allowed us a moment to go and speak with Mr. Limaj because it was apparent that there was a little concern about the plan we had. And of course, given the fact he's in the witness box, we haven't spoken to him about the difficulties we faced with Mr. Churcher and -- not at all in fact. So we explained what the difficulties were. We did not speak of any of the matters he's been deposing to in front of you. But I think you will understand that there is after all this time an anxiety to move on as fast as possible. So the compromise is that he will have another session with Mr. Whiting, if I can put it that way. And then the last session today will mark the beginning of Mr. Churcher, with a bit of argument. I hope it won't take long, and then Mr. Churcher will commence. And I think so we're still confident he will finish by the end of tomorrow. There are nods from the other side. So I'm sorry to slightly re-arrange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does that indicate that it would not be desirable for us to deal with the foreshadowed objection now but it would be better to leave it until after the next break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That's right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Whiting, you better get underway, by the sounds of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No problem. Always ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We might finish the session a little earlier than usual, though, if you find a convenient time at about 20 past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. It's just become convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, we were talking about your visits to Lapusnik. Do you recall -- you testified that on one occasion - and you believed it was after the battle of the 17th and 18th of May, 1998 - you went to a kitchen that soldiers were using at that time nearby, and your best memory was that it was nearby the position 1 or at the top of the rock, guri. Do you remember testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During your subsequent visits in June and July, do you recall becoming aware of another location where soldiers would -- in Lapusnik would gather to eat?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was practical, Mr. Prosecutor. Of course soldiers ate somewhere. Concretely, I don't know, but of course soldiers ate somewhere. The case that I mentioned, it was in the beginning, it was an improvised kitchen. It wasn't a kitchen in the full sense of the word. Two or three school desks were joined together and they served as a kitchen. It was immediately after the battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm talking about June and July now. Do you recall ever going to such a place in Lapusnik where soldiers typically gathered to eat?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. It's not that -- whether I remember it or not, but I know that I did not eat in such kitchens. At that time, we had created a certain relation with some villagers that we didn't know from before. As I mentioned earlier in my testimony, at Sopi's house I used to stop and have a coffee or tea. I have done the same thing on the other part of the terrain where we would go somewhere for a visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just to be clear your testimony is you would not go to the place, wherever it was in Lapusnik, where soldiers were gathered to eat during June and July of 1998. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, to my knowledge, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Ferat Sopi's house or compound -- it was a compound. Correct? Ferat Sopi had a compound?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Qerkin Sopi. Listen, Mr. Prosecutor, you have probably visited Kosovo. Your tradition is that we have big families. Two, three brothers, they live together within the same courtyard. All the courtyards are surrounded by walls. And within those walls, there are two, three, four houses. The same thing was with my family. My family had two, three, four houses in one courtyard. One house served as a guestroom. Usually when visitors came they would go there. And the other part served as bedrooms. The same thing was with Qerkini's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's refer -- you've called it a courtyard. Let's refer to it as a compound. And were -- were -- was Ferat Sopi's house and Qerkini Sopi's house in the same compound or were they different compounds?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't in the same courtyard, Mr. Prosecutor. I cannot refer to it as a compound; I will refer to it as part of our tradition. Let's say one house is of the head of Sopi family and the other houses are also part of the Sopi family.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I need a word that will refer to a group of houses surrounded by a wall. I'm offering the word "compound." If you have a different word, please tell me. Just so we can understand each other with these questions.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Compound is okay?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let it be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Ferat Sopi's house was in one of these compounds, was in a courtyard surrounded by a wall?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's what I'm saying because I cannot refer to it according to your way. The houses within the walls are of Qerkini Sopi's. And these are the houses of his sons. And Ferat Sopi's house is separate, it's outside the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Ferat Sopi's house had no wall around it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I'm not quite sure because as you pass by Qerkin Sopi's courtyard, as you go to his house there is a small hill, ridge. And the nature itself allowed him not to build a wall there. On the part below, behind his house, I don't know whether there was a courtyard or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there two roads that went by Ferat Sopi's house, one that was a little bit above the other one on the ridge? One road in front of the house and one road in back of the house?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will describe it to you now, how I went there. Mr. Prosecutor, you can enter Qerkin's house through his courtyard. And from the upper part, you can go to Ferat's house. There are two gates. From Qerkin's courtyard, you could go to Ferat's house. So when I went to Ferat's house, I passed through Qerkin's courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You described some vineyards where you would sit and drink coffee. Were those behind the house, in front of the house? Where were those in relation to the house?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The place that I visited -- now, I don't know if Ferat has another house or not. There was a sort after a terrace, a balcony, in front of the house and it looks to the mountains. The view is on the mountains, and that's why I'm telling you that I don't know whether there was a courtyard. I don't know whether there was a wall, but from the vineyards, the view is directly on the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the mountains you're referring to -- it's not the ridge where the positions were but the mountains -- the big rock -- the big mountain is what you're referring to? When you say the views of the mountains, you're talking about --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yeah yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Which mountains are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the ridge. It's in the direction of the position, to my knowledge. From there you can see them, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if Ferat Sopi's house was destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I was never there, Your Honours, because the majority of villagers after the war left. And not only from that village, from the neighbours villages as well. Some settled in cities, in towns, and some got apartments and basically they didn't go back because they maybe had nothing to go back to. Their houses were destroyed. So to tell you the truth, I don't know what happened after the war because I was never there. After the war, there was a great movement of the population; they moved from one place to another, and this happened with the majority of the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer is: I don't know?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, yesterday we looked at an article -- it was an interview -- it's not an article. It's a transcript of an interview that you gave to Albanian television on the 3rd of June, 1998. It's Prosecution Exhibit 37, and we had a -- the translation was incomplete. We've -- we now have a complete translation and I ask that it be put in front of you so we can just finish -- complete talking about that. Do you remember that we talked about this yesterday? Now, the part that I wanted to focus on that wasn't on the translation yesterday was -- there's a question which was: "Can you tell us something about the actual results of this resistance?" And your answer is: "The greater part of the Drenica territory and of Llapushe in general is free and under the control of our forces, that is, under the UCK's control. Our forces have had control of the Pristina-Peja highway for one month now starting with the checkpoint at Komorane and further." That's what you said in the interview. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the second question.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That's what you said in the interview. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it was true? What you said there was true?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did explain the developments, the Lapusnik gorge fell. There was a great battle. The road to Malisheve was blocked, and part of it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Just -- the sentence I read just now, that's true, what you said, the second answer? That's true?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. "Our forces controlled the Peja-Pristina road for a month now from Komorane checkpoint onwards" -- no, no. Not the checkpoint at Komorane, that belonged to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means from the gorge, from Lapusnik gorge and onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And then you were asked -- the next question that you're asked is: "We have received reports that you are increasingly supported by the native population there. Can you tell us something more specific about this phenomenon." And your answer is: "Like everywhere else in Kosovo, in Drenice and Llapushe as well, we have encountered full support on the part of the population of this area who has put everything at the disposal of the war. Thus in Kosova the people and the UCK are one in the same just as flesh is joined to the bone." Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was that true?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained this, Mr. Prosecutor, as I described it earlier after the 29th euphoria -- not 29th, it was even earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm not asking you to repeat yourself. I'm just asking is that true, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that the translation that is with the exhibit is incomplete. If this complete translation, Albanian translation, could be substituted or added in with the exhibit, that would be appreciated. It's P37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Defence have a copy, do they?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, if that could be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll arrange that with the registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you testified that "Some people might pretend today" -- you're talking about Lapusnik and you said that: "Some people might pretend today that they weren't there, that they never visited the place." Do you recall saying that, that --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that -- and that's because there was a prison camp in Lapusnik and those who are able to say that they weren't there will now say that they weren't there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't interpret it this way. This is because of fear that you have instilled in them. Even Ibrahim Rugova was scared that there might be an indictment against him. You, Mr. Prosecutor, didn't allow me to explain about my pseudonym Celiku. I don't know why now we are not going on with the interview. I don't know whether you don't want to hear the truth. I wanted to explain why it was that I got the pseudonym Celiku. You were saying that I was escaping the truth here. From this point, this is a turning point as far as my naming Celiku is concerned, and I want to explain that. You mentioned two matters from that interview, but you're not mentioning the main issue.
