This is the most important moment in this interview as far as my pseudonym Celiku is concerned. And for the sake of the truth, allow me, Your Honours, to explain it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, which interview are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been remarks that I'm speaking too fast. The interview you just gave me, the interview dated 3rd of June and which is directly linked with the pseudonym Celiku, I think that for the sake of the truth I should explain this Trial Chamber what you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, please give your explanation. It relates to this interview that we -- P37 that we were just looking at?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 3rd of June --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What is the explanation that you wanted to give to the Trial Chamber about this interview?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Explanation about Celiku, about the pseudonym Celiku. This is what I want to explain. I want to tell you how I got the pseudonym Celiku. Your Honours, after the battle of the 29th at Lapusnik gorge, a journalist -- the journalist who composed this, who made this interview is Ismet Sopi. I knew him from before because his niece used to study with me in Pristina. And after the battle at Lapusnik, which echoed in Kosova, he came to Klecka to visit me. We sat down, we discussed, and I asked him, Why are you not presenting the KLA properly before the media? And he replied, Well, how shall we do it when nobody is ready to discuss with us, to talk with us? And from this conversation, he insisted that I gave an interview for the Albanian television, for the media. I accepted. We went to a house that had an antenna, a satellite dish, because you had to be in such places in order to have reception with a phone. And what I told him is as follows. I can speak, but I cannot speak with a name. So how shall we do it? And we decided to use one of the KLA commanders as a name. We agreed to use this, that a commander of the KLA is calling from the Drenica zone. And we continued. This was the first time for a KLA member to give an interview for the Albanian television by sound. And, Mr. Prosecutor, this interview was prepared at 5.00 and was broadcast at 6.00, 6.30. When he finished with his questions and I finished with my answers, I was quite emotional - it was a first time I spoke with the media. I went back to my base to listen to the interview. When I heard it on the news, I heard that they used Commander Celiku. And immediately the following day I found this journalist and I asked him, What happened, Ismet? He said to me that the editorial board in Tirana did not accept for this interview to be broadcast without a name of the person who was being interviewed. And he said he decided to use that name because he had heard from the radio Celiku 1, Celiku 2, Celiku 3, and that's why he decided to choose that name so that the interview could be broadcast. I want to add that this was heard in Kosova and the diaspora because the interview was mainly for the diaspora because they had the dilemma whether there was or was not a KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just have one more second and I'll be finished. So the diaspora then used this interview in their gatherings because it was the only document in Albanian. So they used this interview in order to raise funds. And when people started to come to Kosova from the diaspora, whoever came wanted to meet Commander Celiku because that's what they heard on TV and on these gatherings for fund-raising. And this is how it started. And again, with my soldiers and amongst my soldiers, I was known as Daja, with the pseudonym Daja. This is what I wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, this was broadcast on television. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see it here that he did not address me with any other name, that that was added in the editing as the journalist described to me. They added the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I want to be clear on your position. Is your position that there could have been a prison camp in Lapusnik and you did not know about it, or is it your position that there was no prison camp no Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for my position, I would like to explain here before the Honoured Judges that I was shocked when I saw the indictment. I would like to say, based on myself and my views, I had never seen or heard about such a camp. And what is more, I was never a witness to such developments. There was no prison camp in Lapusnik, as you allege. And I'm saying this from my own experience, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to give back to you the pseudonym sheet that -- so that I can refer to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if I could have the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you see the Witness L-07?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You heard the testimony of Shukri Buja, who said that he went to Lapusnik to obtain the release of L-07.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain how that would be possible if there was no prison in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I heard Shukri's testimony. And even without hearing his testimony, out of my own experience, as for detentions, one or two days, tops, they happened everywhere. And this is how I saw it, as things that could have happened. And I believe that this is what Mr. Buja intended. Such things happened everywhere. People were being stopped. Your Honours, my -- my father-in-law was stopped for six or seven hours because he was coming from another territory, and until it was verified that he was coming to me nobody was allowing him to proceed with his journey. So things -- such things might have happened. This is how I looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, the truth is that you yourself were involved in the release of L-07, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, never. I have never seen that person in my life until he came here. I never saw him in my life and I never participated in his release. I only saw him when he came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Shukri Buja vouched for him, and based on that vouching you ordered him released?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I said that I saw that person for the first time here. It is true what -- that Mr. Buja said that here, but that is not the truth. Mr. Prosecutor, you want to make me a criminal in three months, but you cannot do it because facts speak differently. Please, I saw this person for the first time here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You made him write a statement that he wouldn't say anything about Lapusnik or he would be killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. Look at my biography. Why didn't I continue that after August? Such a criminal, such a person, dealing with such matters will have a history of doing such things. These are stories. For me, it's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, can you tell us who a person by the name of Naim is? That's N-a-i-m.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could Mr. Limaj be shown Prosecution Exhibit P30, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, these are notes that were --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Sorry. Wait a second. [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: They were found in your house in a storage room next to the kitchen in your apartment in a search at the time of your arrest. They're signed -- they have the name Naim on them. Can you tell us now who Naim is?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know him. There's nothing else I can say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did these notes get into your apartment?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, after we left, Mr. Prosecutor, after we entered Pristina when the KFOR and NATO forces entered Pristina, the Defence Ministry, because I was a spokesperson for that ministry, that ministry is located 10 metres away from my home, in front of my home. That is where the ministry is and the General Staff and various sectors are. But because that building had formally been an insurance company which left and until they could not find the location where to keep the documentation, the documentation was kept in my house because it's across the road from my home. Instead of taking them away somewhere in some other place far away, they decided to keep the documentation in my house. That's the only explanation I can give. And that's why they found this document in my home, but there is -- I have nothing to do with this document. This is the truth or the explanation I can give you, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, do you recall the other documents that were found in your home?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, various documents were found. Yes. People in their homes have various documents, keep various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall some identifications that were found in your home of -- your identifications?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall where those were stored?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, on the first page of this document, if you look at the first page, is the name Lutfi Xhemshiti.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It refers to Lutfi Xhemshiti and his four children.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know that Lutfi Xhemshiti was kidnapped from his house in Breg i Zi on 30 July 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about one thing and that is from the indictment that I read. I never heard about this person before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't know that he was seen in Lapusnik, that his body was recovered in Berisha? You don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, for the first time -- or the first time that I heard about this was when I read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's just a coincidence that a document with his name on it is found in your apartment? That's just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain what the issue of the documentation was like. There is no other explanation for it. I kept documentation for the ministry at my home because it's only 10 metres away from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what other documents you kept for the ministry or what other kinds of documents?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry had one floor, occupied one floor, of the building. And the other floors were occupied by the General Staff. And there were -- these were documentations about the martyrs, about the veterans, how many members of the General Staff there were, how many soldiers and weaponry they had after demilitarisation. On the second floor there were other sectors, sectors of the General Staff who were located there because they had no other location. The company had to move from that place, so what we had to do was get the documentation and store it. There was no place to store it, so I, together with other people, took some documentation and stored the documentation in our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you store it, this documentation, that you say you stored? Where in your house did you store it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people in the staff of the ministry took it away and left it, possibly, in the balcony or in one room. They put it there. They tried to put it where they would not be an obstacle to our everyday living. In fact, it was my wife who told them where to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So my question is -- my question is: Where in your apartment was this documentation stored? And your answer is that it was in the balcony or in one room?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said there was documentation in the balcony or other places, but it -- because the apartment is a small apartment, my wife told me -- told them where to store it, where to put it. It's only 75 metres -- square metres, sir, so it's a small place to live in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can -- it's important. Can you tell me where in your apartment it was stored, this documentation. Was it stored all together? Was it stored in different places?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am trying to explain. I'm trying to help you. This is something that I did not pay too much attention to. These were documents that were left temporarily at my place. This documentation was left, sometimes part of it in the storage room, part of it in the balcony. Even the computer was left in the balcony until we found another place to put it. I'm trying to help you. The only thing I can say is that we put the documentation in places where they would not be an obstacle to our everyday living. We lived there. There were 13 of us, my father, my mother, there were my brothers and their children, and it was such a small place to live in for so many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This document was found in the storage room next to the kitchen. Were there other documents like the ones you describe in the storage room next to the kitchen, according to you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I'll say it again. There might have been other documentation there from the ministry or other documents, because the storage room is a place where they could leave it for longer time because it was not an obstacle for us to live there. You have it in your pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were these documents kept in boxes or folders or how were they kept?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, I don't know. They were in binders or boxes. Of course it must have happened to you to move office, to go from one office to another, and you put things in boxes. But at that time we did not have all those means, so they did what they could. This was immediately after the war in 1999 and we did not have many things. We did not even have notebooks. So this was immediately after the war, Mr. Prosecutor. It was the beginning, and those documents were there from that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, if you could look at the second page of the document, please, and it's the second page in the English. There's a line -- it's the -- it's the third entry. If you see the little dashes, and it says "Zejn Petrova, always stays" -- do you see? It's the second page.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the numbers in written -- written in blue?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's the number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The third entry down is "Zejn Petrova, always stays with a" -- and the word is written "Shka [sic]" "with a Serb"? "Shka" is -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's a derogatory term for a Serb, isn't it, Mr. Limaj, "Shka"?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The next entry says -- if you could look at it it says: "Syle Llugiqi goes to work at 7.30 and stays at his work until 10.30 and then sits in the 'Galerija' pizzeria until 1030. Always drinks coffee. Generally goes with a Serb (I don't know his name) and then goes back to work. Comes out at 1430 and goes home via road to Konjuh in white Lada Samara." And his licence plate is given. Then it says, "At 1630 Syle goes out in the town (Lipjan) again and goes again to the 'Galerija' pizzeria and sits there with a Serb who works for Lipjan SUP... I don't know his name." And the next entry is: "Syle sat with that criminal of the Serbian police in the 'Napoli' pizzeria from 2000 until 2100 on 2 November 1998."

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your testimony is that you know nothing about this record or what this is referring to. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I know nothing about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation for why the KLA would retain such a document which appears to be -- on its face which appears to be monitoring the movements of somebody meeting up socially with a Serb?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to speculate here. You must look at the zone or region referred to here, where this Zek or Zec [as interpreted] or wherever he is from lived and the intelligence services there. There is no other explanation. The place referred to, they know what they mention by this. It's part of their job, the intelligence services job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- turning to page 3 -- actually page 5 -- page 3 on the English. It's -- there's a date it's about a third of the way down the page it says "3 November 1998." And it says, "There is a plan to kill an Serbian woman but the KLA has to be asked before the matter is carried out." And it says, "Will you ever release that Serbian woman? Is she coming to you because she wants to or by force? What age is she? Did they introduce themselves as people authorised by the KLA?" Is it your testimony you know nothing about what this refers to?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you think, Mr. Prosecutor, that everything that happens in Kosova I know about? These are things that the intelligence services dealt with and they -- you are making me commander of intelligence services, commander of the KLA, everything. I have no idea who made these notes. Look at the date, 3rd of November, 1998. While the victim or the massacre, according to you, happened in July. I have no idea about the things you're mentioning here. I don't know personally anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you have talked about collaborators. You've said nothing about Serb civilians. You would agree with me, wouldn't you, that there is no justification for kidnapping, detaining, maltreating, torturing, or murdering civilians during wartime, wouldn't you? You would agree with me on that, Serb civilians or any other type of civilian?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree, and not only that -- but, Your Honours, look at my biography. From the time I've been a commander of that brigade, you cannot find a single case of a civilian -- of a Serb civilian or Albanian civilian that has been kidnapped or maltreated or tortured during the time that I was a commander of the brigade, and you have an example of how I behaved with the Serbs, the Tanjug journalist. You're trying here to present a systematic case. Tell me about one case when a Serb house has been attacked by me or a case of violence against a Serb house against [as interpreted] me. I have always tried for these things not to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll get to that subject in a moment, Mr. Limaj. Finally, the last entry is -- it's on your page 5, our page 3 -- "Qerim Hamiti, lecturer from the Faculty of Mining Engineering --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I apologise to the translators and the transcriber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "I talked to him about the collaborators about the enemy in our faculty. Qerim is someone who has given a lot of help to the KLA and he is totally trusted regarding cases of the spying of Albanians who work with the enemy." Now, this sounds like a very different type of collaborator than the one that you defined for us during your testimony. Would you agree with me, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say again that these are different circumstances. Each unit wanted to have more information about the developments. With regard to collaborationists, I told you what my position is. This is a summary of different information, pieces of information. Look here, Mr. Prosecutor, it says "faculty" and it's in Pristina. There was no other faculty but the one in Pristina. And here, this is about developments in Pristina. Of course everybody wanted to have more information, but I don't know who was looking for this information. It was not part of my job. I did not deal with that. And I can give you a concrete example. There was Serbs who can -- who gave us information, a general, a Serb who was member of the General Staff of the Serbian army who was fired by Milosevic after the Bosnian and Croatian conflicts, and he was dissatisfied with the Milosevic regime and he contacted Albanians abroad and gave them information. And quite by chance, because members of the General Staff could not meet him, they -- he tried to contact me. Jashar Selihu was the one who told me he would come and meet me. And we had that meeting, Mr. Prosecutor, in Shale. He came in the evening, he gave me some documents, it was just 20 minutes, and then he left. I gave those documents to the General Staff. These things happened from both sides. And this document later was known as the horseshoe document, but I didn't know at the time what they referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you know that on the 12th of July, 1998, in that interview that we looked at before that Jakup Krasniqi gave from Klecka? Remember that interview that we looked at from the 12th of July, 1998? You --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The picture with Shukri and the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct. It's in P -- Exhibit P48 and P49. Do you remember - and I can show you the interview if you like - but do you remember that Jakup Krasniqi said --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can look at the interview, Mr. Prosecutor, so that I know which interview you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the witness can be given P49 in the large format. We have it in the large format. The ERN in English is U003-8589 and in the Albanian it's U008-1606.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you have that page?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, if you could look at the third column and the question that is put to Mr. Krasniqi is: "The international community has criticised the violation of human rights and the kidnapping of Serbian and Montenegrin civilians. What can you say about this?" Do you see that question?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Mr. Krasniqi says: "It does" -- and I believe it's on the Sanction. Is it. "It does indeed seem to us ridiculous to equate the operations of the UCK with those of the Serbian occupier which are notorious throughout the world. On this point it seems to me that the international community is not respecting its conventions, starting with the UN charter, because the UCK has never dealt with civilians or only if they have been in the service of the army and the police and have done serious harm to the people and the Albanian national cause. There have been cases in which they have been kidnapped, but in this -- but in this event they have been handed over to the international organisations, of course when they have been innocent. First of all, all Serbian forces whether the police and military armed civilians are enemy." And then it continues: "From the start we have had our own internal rules for our operations. These clearly lay down to the UCK recognises the Geneva Convention and the conventions governing the conduct of war even though it has not been offered the chance of signing them as we would have done. We do not go in for kidnapping. Even if some people suffered, these have been more Albanian collaborators than Serbian civilians. We do not deal with civilians. We return those whom we take as prisoner of wars." And this is the sentence I'm particularly interested in and going to ask you some questions about: "A few days ago we handed over two Serbs originating from Croatia to the International Red Cross. Those we have kidnapped are either announced on a list -- but we do not behave in a base fashion like Serbia." The two Serbs that he is referring to, Mr. Limaj, was -- were the Bakracs. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be. It could be them. However, it's not specified here who they are, but they could be the ones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know that they were kidnapped in Carraleve on the 30th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where they were kidnapped from and I don't know either where they were sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't know that they were taken to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi -- you never talked to Mr. Krasniqi about these two Serbs, what the story was with these two Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This was a time when you testified you were meeting regularly with Jakup Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we met with Mr. Krasniqi, but there were many other things that we talked about, and this was not under my area of responsibility. And maybe he thought I didn't know about it so he didn't talk to me about it. And he had no obligation, in fact, to speak about it with me. There were so many problems at that time that we had to discuss with Mr. Krasniqi, but we never discussed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You never learned that they had been kidnapped in Carraleve and taken to Lapusnik and held in Lapusnik for approximately a week?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I heard it only here from you. I never heard it before, not even in the media. We didn't have newspapers at the time. It was only very rarely that we got any newspapers, and there was about this, about people taken to Lapusnik or away from Lapusnik. The Serbian newspapers spoke about these terrorist actions of Albanians and kidnappings, but I have never heard about this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In fact, you were in Lapusnik when they were there and you were involved in their release. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I told you about my activities. You're trying to place me in Lapusnik all the time, but that's not true. You can say anything you want but there is only one truth, and that is that I never in my life participated in such a camp, and this is my truth, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, the -- when the Bakracs were kidnapped they were kidnapped with two people by the name of Stamen Genov and Djordje Cuk. And a statement written by Stamen Genov and an identification card from Djordje Cuk were found in Lapusnik when the forces went into Lapusnik on the 26th of July, 1998. Do you have any explanation for how those documents got to Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you argue or prove that they were found in Lapusnik, really found in Lapusnik? Can you prove it here that they were found by the Serbs in Lapusnik? The Serbs had everything in their hand. They could do everything they wanted. I read in your exhibits that Stamen Genov was found in Kline. That's what the Serbs say to you and the document says that he was found in Kline. I don't know. I can't explain anything to you about these things. I don't know what the Serbs did. They could do anything. I don't know whether it's true or not. I know what the Serbs did, however. We had such experiences. I can give you thousands of examples of the ways and means they used against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, we've had evidence in this case about three Russian journalists and an interpreter who were stopped at Lapusnik on the 20th of July, 1998. Do you remember that evidence? And they were with Shaban Hoti.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You heard about that at the time, didn't you? You knew about -- that that had happened at the time?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to explain the developments as they happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th, 19th, and the 20th --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please if you could just answer the question. Did you learn about these men -- these journalists being stopped and about Shaban Hoti at the time, on the 20th of July, or shortly thereafter? Did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't. And that's why I was trying to explain how the events unfolded. That was my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When's the first time you heard about it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about this case -- I think his daughter is in Pristina in the Ministry of Defence. I don't remember the name. He was a professor of the university -- at the university. And there are very few of them, so they are known. Somebody from his family came and asked about him --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we go into private session briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You wanted to explain.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. At that time, Your Honours, after people had left and came back to Kosovo, many people had disappeared and members of their families came to various institutions or various bodies to learn about them. They came also to the Ministry of Defence. They said this-and-this person, we lost him, we don't know where he is. Do you know anything about him? And I told them, as I said to many other people, We don't know. Go to the International Red Cross, go to other organisations, they might know more. Or maybe go to the General Staff because they might know more, especially the zone commanders might know more about these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I remember this because it was mentioned there that he was a professor. That's why I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And so -- just to be clear, your testimony is: After the war somebody from the family came to inquire -- ask you about this person. Is that correct? Just to be clear about your testimony. This was after the war --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was right after the war in 1999 I think it was, or maybe 2000. 1999/2000, after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm not going to go through all the other victims in the case because your position is that there was no camp, that there was no mistreatment, no torture, no murders. So I'm not going to go through with you all the other items. I'm going to move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm so sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, you have stated then a position that I don't believe I've gathered from the evidence so far. Now, is that your point, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your position is that there was no camp in Lapusnik in June and July of 1998, and therefore no mistreatment there of prisoners, no torture of prisoners, no murder of prisoners in Lapusnik. That's your position. Correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are putting it on me is making me very sad. I don't think it's a victory just to sentence someone, but the victory is also to prove the innocence of someone, Mr. Prosecutor. My sense is this, Your Honours: I was shocked when I heard that. I have never seen, never heard, never in my life have I been involved in such things. That is my answer, Mr. Prosecutor, and I have no other answers to give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For that reason, I won't go through and ask you about the other victims in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I do have more questions but it's now almost 5.20, so perhaps it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll attempt to be brief. In their filing on the 23rd of May, the Defence have -- which I believe Your Honours have -- have given a list of exhibits, additional exhibits, for Fatmir Limaj. The only one I raise issue with is the other, which is an interview conducted by the OTP with Mr. Thaqi. And let me just describe the background to that interview. The interview was tape recorded -- was attempted to be recorded on the 5th of May, 2004. Unfortunately there was an equipment failure. There was no recording of the interview. The interview, the essence of the questions and answers asked was then put on paper. There was a meeting with Mr. Thaqi. He made changes, which are indicated in italics, and then all parties signed this as a reconstructed transcript or statement of what occurred at the interview, and it's signed with a, attestation similar to the OTP statement of witness statements. The Defence knew about this interview at some point and requested a copy of it apparently on the 29th of May, 2004. It was not disclosed until 15th of April this year. That was our oversight. I believe that soon before the 15th of April the Defence asked again. We said, Well, we've already given it; we checked and we hadn't. So that's our mistake. My objection to this statement being admitted through Bob Churcher or any other witness is that it is, in fact, a statement; it's a statement of a prospective witness. It's testimony prepared in advance of trial. There are three ways that a witness's testimony can come in before a Chamber in this: Live, 92 bis, or 89(F) under certain circumstances. I have passed out the Milosevic decision of 30th September, 2003, or it's being passed out now, which refers to the Galic Appeals decision of the 7th of June. I haven't passed out Galic because the essence of it is contained in the Milosevic decision. The Galic decision states in paragraph 31 which is quoted several times in Milosevic: "A party cannot be permitted to tender a written statement given by a prospective witness to an investigator of the OTP under Rule 89(C) in order to avoid the stringency of Rule 92 bis." And it continues: "By analogy, 92 bis is the lex specialis which takes the admissibility of witness statements of prospective witnesses and transcripts of evidence out of the scope of the lex generalis of Rule 89(C). But Rule 92 bis has no effect upon hearsay material which was not prepared for the purpose of legal proceedings." This statement was prepared for the purpose of legal proceedings. It is not in that universe of hearsay material which can come in through 89(C) or another way. The Thaqi interview falls squarely within the holding in Galic. It's a reconstructed transcript of a prospective witness prepared for the purpose of legal proceedings. The only difference is that they seek to introduce it through an expert rather than through an investigator. I said Galic was followed in Milosevic; I would direct the Chamber and counsel specifically to paras 9, 12, 13, 18, and the disposition. In short, the Milosevic Chamber endorses the approach in Galic but finds that "Under Rule 89(F) a statement which is not strictly in compliance with 92 bis can be committed if three conditions are met: The witness is present in court, the declarant is available for cross-examination and questioning by the Judges, and attests that the statement accurately reflects his or her declaration of what he or she would say if examined." And they make the point at paragraph 18 that in that case a written statement of a witness can be introduced, although it doesn't strictly comply with 92 bis because it is not being introduced in lieu of live testimony. Now, Mr. Thaqi is not a witness for the Prosecution; we've chosen not to call him. As far as I understand, the Defence does not intend to call him. So there is no way that this statement should come in other than through him coming here and testifying or through Rule 92 bis or somehow 89(F). I'll just say that we have strong reservations with this statement. Parts of it have been contradicted just recently by the testimony of Mr. Limaj. Specifically, Mr. Thaqi --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't know that it would help the Chamber to hear your views upon --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. The last point I would then make is that although this was disclosed late, Mr. Thaqi in the statement - whether it's true or not - states, paragraph 32: "This is the same information that he has already provided to the Defence of Fatmir Limaj." So there's been access to this witness, he says. It's a statement and the idea of getting it through -- in through an expert witness is just an attempt, I would say, to end-run around the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. Now, there is a specific category of hearsay. Witness statements or transcripts prepared for legal proceedings, those do not come in through other witnesses unless the declarant is there to be cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. May I say at once, given the material that the Prosecution almost invariably wishes to put in through other witnesses, whether it's television programmes or whatever, I find it a little bit ironic that the observation is made this is trying to get something in the back door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The shoe is on another foot, is what you're putting, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, the back door is wide at the moment in view of what has happened. However, this isn't an attempt to do that. May I indicate what this is and the status of it as far as our position is concerned. There is -- may I just check that Your Honours have it, a supplementary sheet that certainly has been filed from the expert himself which explains fairly shortly why we seek to put it in. If Your Honours haven't had it, I'll just pause for a moment. It's very short, and I can explain it as you look at it, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One Judge at least has had a chance to look at it, but I certainly have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I just give an introduction to it and then you'll see why -- there are only three paragraphs that are really -- the position is this -- I'm not going into what has gone wrong in this case at this stage. The fact of the matter is: so far as the Defence of Limaj is concerned we did not have a statement or an interview with this particular person, Hashim Thaqi. We didn't have anything like the notes or whatever of the interview that the Prosecution did. We didn't have that. Whatever he may say he thinks he's done in the past, we didn't have it. But we did know, because he told somebody representing the Defence, when declining an interview -- a formal interview with us that he had already given one to the Prosecution; that's why we approached them a year ago asking for it. He was telling us that all he'd to say he'd already told the Prosecution. So we asked for it. There was this delay. That has already been referred to. In fact, the position was this: That Mr. Churcher at the time that he was compiling his report did not have access to these notes of this particular interview. And the time that it was served upon us was after the close of the Prosecution case; that was on the -- the case was closed on the 13th of April. And this set of notes was disclosed on the 15th. At that time our team was in Kosovo and the Churcher report was finalised the day after they returned from Kosovo. And it was only after that -- and he specifies, Mr. Churcher does, in this short statement when he was directed to the Thaqi interview. The significance, therefore, of this is as follows. And he's put it in the last three paragraphs, that there's material in these notes of an interview which entirely confirms the view that he'd come to based on other materials. And it's significant, therefore, that somebody in the position of Hashim Thaqi, whose name has come up very regularly in these hearings and whose position is well-known to Your Honours as to the role he played from the beginning in relation to the General Staff, that he is alongside others whose names have been mentioned who plainly have been witnesses in this case, and they are significant and important in terms of providing material information upon which this expert can base his opinion and observations. In other words, may I compare it in this way. Supposing Hashim Thaqi, instead of having an interview with the Prosecution in the way that he did had actually put all those observations into a book, we would have been quite entitled to ask this expert to look at the book, just in the same way as you've been asked to look at the Human Rights Watch report and other books for that matter in relation to the Kosovo period 1998/1999. And there would be -- of course the weight to be given to anything said in a book or the weight to be given to anything said in an interview is quite another matter. And Your Honours are very familiar and well-experienced in making an assessment about that material in the longer term. It is just as if this afternoon we were treated to an interview with somebody who is not a witness and in fact a cross-examination has been based on that. Is it not true -- and then the suggestions come out of what is on the television screen. Well, not objecting to that particularly, given the breadth of material that is available to the Tribunal. Now, this material in this way, we say, can be admitted under the rules without breaching anything and without going behind anybody's rulings in any other case, in other words trying the back door route. That is absolutely not the point. Because this person is an expert he is entitled to look at a whole range of materials and particularly where he is able to say, Well, I had come to these conclusions well before I even saw this interview and the interview confirms, and the features that are confirmed are set out in that supplementary statement, and if you need to be directed to the paragraphs in the Thaqi interview that support those opinions, of course I'm well able to do that if you need it. We say, therefore, that the routes that have been described this afternoon by which materials may be placed before you are not limited in the way that has been indicated. In other words, the three ways was: Live, 92 bis, and 89(F). Well, in fact we would say that it isn't restricted in that way. The first point we'd make, and I make it quickly, is that 92 bis is in fact premised on a of factors even before one gets to the safeguards and other provisos set out further down. Basically, the Trial Chamber may admit in whole or part the evidence of a witness -- well, may I pause. He is not a witness, either for the Prosecution obviously because they haven't called him and I make it clear because we have already obviously served of this, nor for the Defence. So this isn't evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement in lieu of oral testimony. That's not the point. It isn't being tendered or received, whichever word one wants to use, in that context. 92 bis, therefore, is not engaged. I appreciate that the authorities here are saying that it is a prohibitive section. In other words, if it is engaged, then it's only within the parameters of 92 bis that a statement may be admitted. But if it's not engaged, one has to return, in our submission, to the basic general rule or lex generalis, namely Rule 89. Now, Rule 89, looking at the other ways in which the Prosecution are indicating, is not limited to 89(F) because -- and of course the Galic case has a discussion about it; there's 89(C) which as it's worded does not have any restrictions on it. "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." And as you are aware, probative value plainly has to do firstly with relevance - that goes without saying as s it's an earlier part of that rule - and clearly you would have to look at the way or the manner in which it's been obtained. Well, there's no doubt about the provenance of this and it was conducted by the Prosecution themselves as part of their investigation. And clearly one would have to look at some of the content in order to weigh up whether it has not, as it were, definitive probative value but whether it has some probative value. No one is therefore saying it has to have probative value throughout. And of course on occasions what the Prosecution are asking the Tribunal to do in relation to some witnesses is to say, well, some of what they say is true well some of what they say isn't true. The same applies to this. Some of what this gentleman has told the Prosecution may be true and some may be false. But that's beside the point. There is probative value, and we say there is particular probative value when the coincidence is that it accords with an expert, independent view arrived at by looking at other documents. So that's the purpose of this. And we say that it does not as it were triggered or does not trigger itself 92 bis. It comes in, as we say, under 89(C), that you have that broad discretion to allow in the context of an expert to look at a document such as this. So that's the way we put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you sit, Mr. Mansfield, do we take it that it is tendered on your submission in anticipation of the witness being called or is there no intention to call Mr. Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I make it quite clear: He's not on our list. We do not intend to call him. And I also make it quite clear I don't have any interview or statement of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So do we understand the purpose of its tender would be to establish the truth of the facts it contains?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Not entirely, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what the word "entirely" means there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, obviously, to fulfil that function I would have to call him. I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, then, you say, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- force does it have in support of the opinion of an expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- if it contents are not established?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: The same as a television interview being shown to Mr. Limaj this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid there are some leaps in logic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: There are a few, yes. The point is this: If it is to be countenanced - which it is, and it was with the Human Rights Watch and a number of other examples - that material may be placed before this Tribunal which is not coming directly from any witness but it is material concerned with the conflict - and I put that as in inverted commas for the moment because that is the subject of the next witness - but is relevant to the conflict, has been written about the conflict, and there's been numerous interviews which the Prosecution have put in not just with Fatmir Limaj but a large number of other people who are not witnesses. Now, on what basis is that being put in? It's being put in not necessarily to prove the total truth because to do that they would have to call all the people concerned and they haven't called any of them and we haven't objected. It would be a matter for how much weight you attach to material that's coming in via a television interview or via book when you don't have the author. So for example, there was a book put to Mr. Limaj. They are not exhibiting it. And I'm not -- if it comes to it, I'm not suggesting necessarily that this interview -- sorry, notes -- should be exhibited. But I do require the facility to be able to demonstrate that this expert having come to conclusions is able to say Not only did I come to these conclusions when I looked at an interview conducted by the Prosecution with a person who is central to events in Kosovo throughout the whole of this period and still is to some extent, I found considerable corroboration for certain parts. And then obviously it would be a matter for Your Honours to decide whether those certain parts which you would then have to look at obviously, but not obviously in the context of all of it, you would look at the certain parts and decide whether the certain parts that he's talking about which are corroborated by other people and other materials he's looked at then lends some weight -- so to that extent I use the words "not entirely" -- lends some weight of the subsequent material, so they have to be seen together. So it's an exercise you're familiar with having to do. I make it clear, I'm not suggesting it can be regarded as foolproof or the total truth. One can't do that any more than one can with an interview any more than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question is whether it can be regarded as any evidence, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well then, the same applies to the television interviews, I'm afraid. What I would submit is it's material to which you can have regard, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, a number of matters to which you've referred are matters that were done in the course of cross-examination of a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I think that is a very different position from the one you're attempting to sustain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, interestingly -- yes. Anticipating something, I think. But may I say straightaway, some of the materials I'm mentioning, in fact, didn't only arise in cross-examination. In other words, it was the Prosecution in their opening was suggesting that materials such as -- and they were quoted in interviews and so forth, even though at that stage provenance and so on wasn't gone into. The question of weight comes much later. So in a sense, although there is a logical leap and I understand your point that a lot of it does come out of cross-examination, but it is not entirely cross-examination provenance. Some of this material is coming out, as it were, as part of the Prosecution case. Now, when you have examples such as that, then I think -- the Human Rights Watch is an obvious example. They haven't called anybody who actually compiled the report. If you remember, the person who came was an editor of the report and wasn't able to speak to some of what's in it. But you're being asked to look at it. I haven't objected to that, your being asked to look at it. That's a fair enough observation. How much weight you attach to it in the end I think you yourself passed that observation at that time we were dealing with it with that particular witness. So I do make that comparison. And plainly, we say that this is a matter for you to decide in the long run as to whether this is material that assists you or not. But if it were a marginal figure in this case, then obviously I wouldn't even attempt it. But he is a crucial figure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which neither side is intending to call.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you will appreciate that one distinction in addition to what I have mentioned between the matters such as Human Rights Watch report and others was that there was no objection to their admission. There is an objection to the admission of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Or this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we are forced then to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: But then in -- yes, I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's a slight question of admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I say this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It doesn't deny your propositions about weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No. And also whether there's an objection or not doesn't actually make a difference as to whether it's admissible. Because in fact had you yourselves taken the initiative -- I'm not saying you should -- but had you thought at the time Oh, we're not having this, you could have stepped in and said no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We could shorten this case a great deal, Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If we were to be that interventionist in the absence of some glaring breach of the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm accepting that as an approach as it being perfectly reasonable to do that. And therefore we say it isn't the existence of an objection that makes the difference, only that you're forced to look at it. But I can't take it further than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm not overlooking Mr. Guy-Smith, but Mr. Topolski has leapt to his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: It's been so long since you've heard from me, I thought that you might be missing. [Albanian on English channel]... deploy some of this material in cross-examining Mr. Churcher which I intend to do. And consequently my submission would be, if I'm required to make it, that different considerations apply, before I cross-examine and before Mr. Nicholls does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Does your case differ from that of Mr. Mansfield's client in any respect upon which you would be cross-examining?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No, save that the considerations that apply to a cross-examiner differ in important respects to that which applies to an examiner-in-chief, particularly where one is dealing with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a statement that isn't universal, you realise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I appreciate that, but it's certainly one that has been adopted during the course of these proceedings; throughout them, if I may respectfully say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mean we haven't taken umbrage at some of your questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I don't think Your Honour has taken umbrage any of my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I have had horse whispers on either sides of me at times, isn't this cross-examination and leading, and we have let you go on in peace, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I shall let Your Honour live with the expression horse whisperers when this case rises for the evening. But Your Honours are right, I have noticed an absence of interventions as far as I am concerned but that's because I always obey the rules. That's not been necessarily so elsewhere. But, Your Honours, seriously speaking, I would propose that I would be entitled to ask Churcher two things: One, are you aware of this -- the existence of this material -- three things; three, have you read it; four, does it impinge in any way upon conclusions that you have reached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: His answer would be: Well, if its contents are correct then it's consistent with my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And Your Honour gives that answer whatever weight you give it. It is not an inhibition, an embargo upon me introducing it in that respect. For if we are very careful --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question that is the obstacle to you doing that is whether with co-accused your cases can be distinguished on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I would be on stronger ground if this is what we call in my jurisdiction a cut-throat defence. Much stronger. We don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We don't know. One never knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that we should continue, perhaps in contrast to Mr. Mansfield, to rest lightly on technical objections unless they are positively raised and let you ask those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, thank you for the way out. The answer is: Yes, please. But I -- Your Honour doesn't give me a way out that is not enshrined in the rules of this Tribunal. What else could the words "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value added to," in (f), "A Chamber may receive the witness of a witness orally or where the interests of justice allow in written form". Do the interests of justice permit me to ask Churcher whether his conclusions have been affected by, strengthened by, or if he gives me the wrong answer, weakened by what is in the Thaqi interview? And that is why I rise before Your Honours rule upon Mr. Nicholls's application and Mr. Whiting's response, clear in the knowledge that I would propose to cross-examine. Of course if your ruling is against Mr. Mansfield, then it doesn't necessarily end it as far as I am concerned, but I invite Your Honours to give a ruling as to the ambit, if any, of any cross-examination on the point. Thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You come as a sweeper, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A wonderful position to be in. First of all, to be perfectly clear, and I believe I speak also for Mr. Topolski in this regard, I have never received any information from Mr. Thaqi. There have been no interviews with him. So I think all members of the Defence remain in the same position. I think this is important. I think you've been offered two perfectly reasonable and appropriate methods to consider this evidence. One is under 89(F) -- I'm sorry, under 89(C) as relevant evidence, one is under the methodology of cross-examination, which once again takes this same principles into account.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The third one, that it might not actually be tendered in evidence was Mr. Mansfield's proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It might not actually be tendered in evidence. But I think as you would put it the issue has been well ventilated and we trust that you will come up with the appropriate decision in this regard and have this evidence introduced under 89(C) or some other fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, gentlemen. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll be very brief, Your Honour. Mr. Mansfield may not like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we've taken 25 minutes of the precious time of the witness so far, but I'm sure I'm partly responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield might not like the Galic decision at paragraph 31, but he's completely missing the point that statements, material created for the purposes of legal proceedings are not the same as books, they are not the same as articles. They are a different animal. They are not within 89(C). If something is tendered to corroborate then it necessarily has to be offered for the truth of the substance, otherwise it's meaningless. If the expert says Yes, I've read this and it's exactly what I say, and what I say is true because what this says I believe to be true. And third, just I agree with Your Honour's point, cross-examination, this is being offered to corroborate; that's the purpose. That simply because there are several accused, it does not allow one to corroborate through cross-examination. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield, is this point to be reached this evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid it is. I make it very clear, I have to the Prosecution as well. I'm going to be remarkably brief, so I'm afraid it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I would indicate at the moment the Chamber's view is that we would receive the statement as marked for identification and allow you to examine on it on that basis. But that leaves it not as evidence as to the truth of its content and just so that you appreciate. Yes. Your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Churcher, please, I think he's just outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon or evening I suspect Mr. Churcher. Sorry you've been delayed. Would you be kind enough to read aloud the affirmation on the card that is put before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you'd sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Churcher, I'm sitting over here. If you wouldn't mind answering a few questions from me and maybe a few more from others. Is your name Robert Andrew Churcher?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And are you currently a security sector consultant, also training in the same areas as well as being a political analyst?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And I want before just dealing very briefly -- you've tendered a report already which the Tribunal has before them. It runs to 30 pages and I'll come to the issue that it addresses in one moment. But before I do that, may I just with certainly I hope no objection just lead you as to your background just one or two matters only because it's all written out in great detail. But what may be of importance so far as the Tribunal is concerned is your experience vis-a-vis the Balkans. But can I put generally: You've had over 30 years experience in security matters and I'll deal with how that's divided up. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And the -- if I may put it, the starting point which we can find on page -- may I use the pages at the top, 5372. Do you have a copy of your own report in front of you? I think perhaps you should have.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I don't, I'm afraid, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: All right. Well, I think it's important that you have the same that we have. You won't have the page, but I'm sure you'll be familiar. I just wanted to indicate that you were an officer in the British army for 23 years, having served in five different operational tours of duty in that time. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you were awarded an MBE, a Member of the British Empire award for your work in field intelligence with regard to that service?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And after that, that is after your military service - again I'm going to summarise it - between 1993 and 2002, in other words nearly ten years, you have consistently worked from time to time in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That is also correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And you specify a number of organisations, I'm not going go through them all, but they are not only international organisations such as the United Nations and the European Union but also different governments.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, so far as the Balkans are concerned, you have in fact been to Kosovo on a number of occasions, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I have. I have also worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And just looking so that the Tribunal can see what I'm asking looking at, it comes in the curriculum vitae part of your statement towards the beginning, where you've put in boxed form specific relevant country experience, which is paragraph 13, specific relevant country experience under the heading "Kosovo." I'll go a little slower. Sorry. It's my fault. Kosovo in the left-hand column, between September and August of 2001. You were director of an international crisis group dealing with conflict analysis, as is set out there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Just a little further on the same page a period of time before that, that is 1993 -- middle of 1993 until September 1999, again, countries which you were covering during that period of time for all the organisations you've put on the right-hand side, the European Union and the United States of America government, the United Kingdom government, and so on, covers Albania, Macedonia, Kosovo, and Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to go through the detail of the rest because under paragraph 14 there are numerous references to Bosnia, Kosovo, Macedonia, and Albania and your work in all those arenas?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, as part of that, were you -- did you take an interest in what may be termed the armed conflict within Kosovo in those years?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I did. From 1993 when I was asked to go to the -- first asked to the Albanian/Kosovo border, I took a strong interest in events in Kosovo from then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this case, as you may know we're dealing with, as far as the indictment is concerned, a particular period of time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Mansfield --

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I've speeded up again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- you're speeding. A break between question and answer would help the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're interpreting into several languages, Mr. Churcher, and there is inevitably a delay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Don't worry. It's entirely my fault because I can't always hear when the translation is finished, but I'll pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the indictment in this case, we're dealing with a particular period in 1998, namely April, roughly speaking, through to August 1998. From the materials provided to you, which you list in your report, and your own experience and observation, what is your overall view about whether there was an armed conflict in that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: My theory is that it was very difficult to say that there was an armed conflict in that period since one of the parties didn't comply, in my view, with the conditions for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And is it right to say that your report indicates what those conditions are?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about that. I want to turn to something that wasn't in your report because you didn't have the material at the time you made it, namely the interview notes with a gentleman called Hashim Thaqi. Do you know the matter to which I've --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I've recently seen those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I'm pausing again so that the interpreters are happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Having looked at those interview notes, do they have a bearing upon the opinion to which you had already come?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes. Those interview notes very -- although they were brief very much confirm what I was saying in my report, that there was no coherent or effective middle chain of command at the beginning. People were simply coordinating with each other, and that the whole situation was confused and that you couldn't in any way rely on the communiques which were pure propaganda in most cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And what about the position of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: The General Staff was not a military organisation in the way that its title might indicate, but that it was a collection of individuals who met in different places at different times and who were intending to provide political direction but didn't actually understand what they were doing by way of military command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And again, if it's required, you're able to indicate within the interview notes the paragraphs that support that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I can, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mansfield. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Nor I, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Churcher.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you for coming here. I understand you have to leave tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you tell me briefly what your duties are in Afghanistan, what you're doing there?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I'm working on a British government-sponsored project on governance in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's field work. Can you tell me a little bit more about what actually you do for that project.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I'm actually in Kabul. I have been building a government department which is -- can be brought in use and it's intended to improve the governance of Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that's part of what you refer to in your CV as your expertise, I think you call it on page 5, post-conflict environments?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you've spent a lot of time, as Mr. Mansfield's led you through it, working in the field, what would be called the field?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's, generally speaking, demanding, hard difficult work.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's not the same as a 9.00-to-5.00 office job with every weekend off?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, it tends to be fairly full-time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talked very briefly on the time from 1993 on, 1993 to 1995 I think it was, on your CV, page 5 it says you were in Albania and Bosnian. That's when you were working for ECMM. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can you just tell me from 1993 -- I should probably slow down -- through January 1998, during that period how much time were you actually stationed in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Between -- in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: None whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: None whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Nobody was stationed in Kosovo at that time. It wasn't possible to be stationed in Kosovo at that time. That's why we sat on the border and looked in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I know you have to go back quickly. It's best if you try just to answer my questions. If I need more clarification, I'll ask. You answered that question completely when you said "none whatsoever," but thank you for continuing. How much of that time were you in Albania?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Between -- in 1993, the majority of the time. In 1994, much of the time. In 1995, I went to -- in April 1995 I went to Western Macedonia, which is also Albanian-speaking and obviously has a connection to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to ask you a couple questions, again continuing on your background. August 1997 to January 1998 you were working on the issue of adoptions. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, following on from the Albanian elections, I got asked to negotiate a memorandum of understanding with the Albanian government on adoptions, which was a slightly tricky political issue, which is why I came to it, because adoptions can be very profitable for some people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. That has nothing to do with the KLA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing, but it did keep me in Albania at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. In Tirana?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: In Tirana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One question I want to ask you just to clarify: When were you in Tanzania working on gold-mining security?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: February, March 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Let me say why I ask: Because on your CV on page 2 it says January through June 1998, and on page 4 it says February to May. Do you know, I'm wondering --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
