utterances.text: I was on contract but I got a serious case of malaria and came back to the U.K. This is a World Bank CV which requires you showing what you were doing at all times while you were on contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand. There is this discrepancy about when you left and when you returned to Albania. So were you in Albania in January 1998 and in June 1998 or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I came back in June 1998. I have to say we're talking some considerable time back now, but I think it was about June the 12th. I have to say I'm not entirely certain there, and you'll see I came back to do a security job for Kroll.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that had to do with winding up so-called pyramid schemes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was also busy, demanding work.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That was not busy, demanding work. High-risk, possibly, but a fair amount of time off each day. I mean, I was looking at the overall political risk and security of the thing, which meant spending a lot of time talking to people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you were sort of taking it easy during that period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I don't know if taking it easy is right. It depends on what you regard the stress of security work as.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not talking about stress. I'm talking about the amount of hours you're spending working on these pyramid schemes, how much time it takes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Probably there no more than, on average, half a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just the last question on this point: When you were in Tanzania from roughly January through June 1998, what are your duties there? The CV says "negotiating or reaching agreement or removing indigenous minors in remote rural areas." Could you tell us what that's all about?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: At that time a number of gold-mining companies were interested in low ore rock, I mean low gold content. And they were covered in local miners who were digging in the top 2 or 3 metres. I was brought in there to assist with drilling operations to see what was down deeper and I what I did was negotiate it with local people to say if you move out of the way we can provide a few jobs and we can all get along with each other. We're not going to interfere with you, you're not going to interfere with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, at that time, nothing to do with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Nothing to do with the KLA, but I maintained e-mail contact with contacts in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this report which you wrote, you explained that you did not -- you chose or were unable to heavily cite this report with footnotes and things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No. I mean, I wrote the report on the basis of the fact that I remained interested in what was going on in Kosovo and I continued to follow it throughout that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. And that's where you're talking about on page 2 that you continued to maintain a range of contacts, to keep in close contact with events in the north of Albania and in Kosovo "out of personal interest".

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You also state that from the point of view of writing the paper you were not at that time -- "you were not at the time of the events being considered particularly interested in dates or references." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You weren't paying attention to dates?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Not close attention. I mean, I wasn't sitting there trying to write an academic paper at that time; I was simply maintaining an interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So for the period of January through June 1998, your sources of information are through social contacts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Through social contacts I think would be the right way of describing them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And were rather removed in time as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I obviously caught up when I came back. I watched the situation throughout 1997. Catching up when I came back in June was not very difficult, particularly because I had very close contacts in the north in Bajram Curi and Kukes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So your report then is really not the result of analysis of the situation which you sat down to do once you were tasked by the Defence. You have written down what you remember from that time period?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No. I think if you read my report you'll see that it is analysis based on what I remembered and based on what I knew from that time period plus the sources I was asked to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But it's just -- like I said, it's based on your memory. You've sat down and tried to think about what you remembered and written down what it meant to you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, it's based on my memory and reading informed by that memory. I was one of the people who was on the ground. I had lived in Kukes and I had lived in Bajram Curi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you said informed by what you were asked to read. Asked to read by whom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: By the Defence team. I read a number of things that I was not specifically directed to read, basically the reading which I've quoted there, and I've read widely outside of that. But that was what I decided to pick on here in my notes the sources, although there are many other sources which you could use to back up the same information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We'll talk about what you were given to read a little bit later. Let me talk about some different ways of writing reports. You've read and you cite a Human Rights Watch report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You know the way Human Rights Watch compiles and prepares reports, do you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with the way they write reports, no, and you'll notice, actually, that I -- although I cited it because I think it's relevant, I was a little suspicious of their reporting, their connections, so I didn't use it very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. And that's the 2001 report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, do you agree based on your experience that one way to gather information of a conflict situation is through field work, including interviewing people?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Compiling data?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Using standardised forms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Bringing that data into a database and evaluating the results of it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes. It's not a route that I would choose myself, but it is a route.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You are aware -- you were with OSCE -- that's the way OSCE works?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's not the way they worked while I was with OSCE in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What about the way KVM worked when they were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I didn't work with KVM, as you can see, so it wouldn't be proper for me to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My question is: Do you know how they worked, how they prepared their reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, I didn't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Would you agree it would be helpful to meet with refugees and parties to the conflict at the time the conflict is ongoing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, which of course I did on a large number of occasions. I was responsible for setting up refugee camps and -- in Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At what time?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: As they came across the border. From March 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It would also be useful in compiling a report to talk to KLA commanders on the ground during the conflict in 1998.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That might have been useful, but it wasn't possible for me. I wasn't on the ground in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. But you would agree that if KVM were able to do that, if they were able to do those things, talk to refugees on the ground in 1998, talk to KLA commanders on the ground in 1998, and travel through the area, that would be a good way of preparing an accurate report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: If they had sufficient experience to interpret what they were hearing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me explain to you the way Human Rights Watch prepares reports. They consult with diplomats, NGOs, and specifically Human Rights Watch in this case, Kosovo in 1998; they consulted with Amnesty International. You agree that would be helpful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I would put that into context immediately. Diplomats often spend very, very short periods of time on their posting and even shorter time in country. And as you know, embassies carry out policy, they don't make it. And therefore a diplomat is following a policy based on whatever short-term experience he's got.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But diplomats have access to information that ordinary people do not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Often, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Often, yes. But working with Amnesty International, Humanitarian Law Centre based in Belgrade, the Council for the Defence of Human Rights and Freedoms, an Albanian-based NGO, that would all be helpful while liaising with other people who were on the ground at the time during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In addition, Amnesty -- Human Rights Watch worked with the Kosovo Diplomatic Observer Mission, the Red Cross, and open sources, journalists. That could also be helpful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They don't just talk to those groups, they carry out their own investigations on the ground, talking to victims, talking to soldiers, talking to commanders. That would be useful to understanding the conflict in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Providing they had sufficient background, as I said, to understand what you were hearing and to be able to put that into context.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, assuming we have somebody with a lot of experience and a good background who has travelled in many countries. That would be very useful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It would also be useful to have experience of the build-up to the Kosovo conflict over that relevant period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So you agree that their experience in Kosovo in 1990 would be useful?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I would, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the information you received through your social contacts, how did you corroborate that information with the original sources of the information?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I spent a lot of time travelling on the border, as you know, throughout that period. I built up a wide range of contacts in the north. People came backwards and forwards between Tirana, and out of interest we talked and I followed what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand that. But I'm asking you if you heard from one of your sources, there was a massacre here, this person was injured, the KLA are in this area. Did you at any time speak to the original source of that information to corroborate it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, but you'll also see from my report of course that I wasn't actually following things like massacres. That was not of particular interest. What I was interested in was the way the situation was building up politically and the way it was likely to eventually spill over, which is what we had been looking at since 1993. That was the phrase that continued to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And massacres and crimes that occurred are not relevant?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: They are a matter of news. What I was interested in was the political developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the location of troop movements?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's military intelligence; I didn't have any interest in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You didn't have any interest in that. And the location and movements of KLA units. Did you verify or learn anything to do with that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there were units and I wouldn't have accepted there were units. There were scattered groups who were building up and had been building up in a change which had been taking place from 1996 onwards. But I'm certainly not aware of any units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you a bit about your educational background, if I may.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you been to law school?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Tell me a little bit about your military background. I'd just like to know -- it's not clear to me. I may have missed it on your resume. What rank did you achieve --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I finished as a major in January 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You talk in your report about teaching troops.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Instructing on laws of war and humanitarian law.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes. Very briefly, I might add; ordinary soldiers don't require to know very much, but that's precisely what I taught. But it meant that I had to do some background reading. But we're talking about a period which is more than 15 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's all right. And you anticipated, I was going to say, if you're talking to an ordinary -- you're instructing a private, he needs to know what he's allowed to do, what he's not allowed to do?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I was teaching young officers, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Young officers, how to treat prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: How to treat civilians?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Portionality, civilian objects, that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We talked a little bit about military intelligence. You correct me if I'm wrong, I've never been in the military. I'm learning about it as I go, working here, as much as I can. But basically military intelligence involves an intelligence staff trying to be fed information -- tries to receive information from various reliable sources. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's conventional military intelligence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I'm talking about, conventionally.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That includes attache reports, reports generated by Mr. Crosland, whose testimony you've read?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That would not normally be regarded as military intelligence, but it might be used by people --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I mean. A military analyst might consider those reports along with all the other information.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, but that eventually comes down to considering newspaper articles as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's -- was going to be another question on this. Open-source material would also be included?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It can be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, it is by -- I mean the British military intelligence, doesn't it, when it's reviewing a situation look at all the sources, including open-source material?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Including, yes. It depends on whether you want to source your material or not. But we're going to get a bit technical here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But that is one of the things they look at -- they may look at?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That would depend on the precise nature of what you were doing. It isn't necessarily so at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I know it's not necessarily so at all times. I don't think you need to fight me on this one.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It simply depends on whether you're going to source your material or not. If you're going to source your material you're not going to use that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the other ones are intelligence gathered by operatives, intercepts of signals and communications, and anything that could be gained by aerial photography?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's a material which I'm not -- the intercept material is a field which I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, the VJ at this time in 1998, you'll agree, wanted to know as much as it could about the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as -- the MUP did as well?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Again, I would assume that. You're asking me something outside of my direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if you don't know anything, that's fine. Tell me if I ask you something outside of your knowledge. And the VJ -- well, you talk about the VJ somewhat in your report. What -- do you feel you have any expertise in the capabilities of the VJ to gather intelligence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I won't ask you questions about that. Then you wouldn't really be in a position to dismiss VJ reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, I would not be in a position to dismiss them on military intelligence grounds, but it would -- often to dismiss them on propaganda grounds. If you had spent that much time in the Balkans, you will listened to enough propaganda from VJ or Serbian sources --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Internal --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: And determine what you can dismiss.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That would come under the open-source, though. I mean, a situation report from a commander to his superior, that's not propaganda, that's not ever supposed to be released to the outside world at all.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That depends on what he wants to tell his commander, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now you're speaking very generally, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I'm speaking generally, yes, but having been in the military system, I'm moving slightly away from intelligence matters. When you're sending a report up, what the report up says may well be predicated as what you wish to do as a course of action on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But let's get back to basics. That would not be your ordinary military report has propaganda value. Ordinary military reports up a chain of command are because the subordinate needs to inform the commander of what the situation is on the ground. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Sorry, I've just lost your sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'll ask the question again. Let's talk about the generic military command structure just for a minute. Okay?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When a subordinate sends a report, as required, to his commander, it is an order to give the commander information he needs in order to make decisions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And that information needs to be accurate if it's going to be useful.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: It should be, yes. That depends on whether the commander knows enough, of course, to make it accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, everything depends on the person doing it, but in general that's what reports are about. They're not about propaganda. Right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: That -- as I said, depends on who wrote it and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, when you wrote reports in the military to your superiors, were they propaganda containing statements which were not true or were you truthful in your reporting?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I was truthful in my reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you worked in ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In Tirana and Skopje?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: In Bosnia, in Tirana, and in Skopje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I take it that when you worked in ECMM you wrote reports?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Probably on a regular basis?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: On a nightly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I take it that you did your best to ensure that the information in those reports was accurate and reliable?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you weren't the only person in ECMM who was conscientious that way?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: No, but as you know from ECMM's reputation, who was conscientious and who was not varied very wildly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Which is again the point you've made, that in every endeavour -- in every human endeavour there is the factor of the person doing the job, whatever it is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, how were you selected to be the expert in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I find that that's a rather odd question. I mean -- I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I quite agree, but I thought it would be interesting to hear Mr. Churcher's response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: We drew lots.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to say -- the scapegoat answer is: I don't know that. You've seen what my experience was. I don't suppose many other people have got that comparable experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What I meant was -- and I'm sorry it wasn't a good question, obviously. But what I meant was: What contacted you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: The Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I think some time in November, but I'm not -- I'm not completely clear. It was either late October or November.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And when did you provide the first draft of your report to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: First draft, which was a great deal shorter than this, was in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when you were contacted -- do you remember who it was who contacted you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I think in fact I'd been contacted before that initially by Steven Powles, and who contacted me when it became much firmer I can't answer -- remember the name initially. It was probably Michelle, but I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's fine. And based on that first contact or your first talks, what did you understand your assignment to be? What was the mandate, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: To report on the situation as relating to the command structure of the KLA through the period that I had done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And what were you told to achieve in that report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I wasn't given much direction, actually. I was given a very free hand and I certainly didn't have any specific instruction as to what I was to achieve nor how long it was to be or anything else. It was very much a matter of the two sides exploring each other, to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And -- we're almost done. I just want to ask you the question again. You said "to report on the situation as relating to the command structures of the KLA." Could you flesh that out a little bit. What were you supposed to -- what question were you supposed to answer with this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: The title says it all. What I was asked to do was I was to report on the organisation of the Kosovo Liberation Army and events in Kosova in 1998. And within that -- well, I wasn't given any further direction at all. I was simply asked to use that report. And it was unclear to me at the beginning as to whether there was going to be used or whether indeed it was going to be useful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And you were provided with material which you could use by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: Later on I was provided with a number of transcripts from -- by the Defence and Stephanie Schwander-Seivers' reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You may not know, but were you provided with all the open-session transcripts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I don't know that, I'm afraid. It was certainly a large amount of reading. But that was not until much later on, by which time I was on about draft 17 -- sorry, it would have been draft 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: So that draft 14 they sent you a bunch of transcripts to review?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT CHURCHER
utterances.text: I'm afraid I haven't retained any record of the chronology of what I was sent when. I think if you're going to ask about that we'd have to check. I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's maybe one minute early, but that's good for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We must adjourn now, Mr. Churcher, resuming tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 26th day of May, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.,
